Guinevere. Queen of Britain and wife to King Arthur, Guinevere embodies the tragic contradiction between duty and desire. Her forbidden love for Lancelot, the greatest of Arthur's knights, becomes the catalyst that unravels the fellowship of the Round Table and precipitates Camelot's fall.

She was beautiful and accomplished, the epitome of courtly grace and medieval queenship at Camelot. Her passionate affair with Lancelot was discovered and publicly exposed, causing irreconcilable shame and political crisis. The revelation fractured the Round Table, forcing many of Arthur's greatest knights to choose sides. Lancelot rescued her from execution, an act that turned loyal knights against him and against Arthur. Some versions depict her as entering a convent in her final years, choosing religious penance and withdrawal from the world.

Guinevere represents the central tragedy of Arthurian legend: that even the noblest ideals cannot survive human passion and flawed judgment. She is often portrayed sympathetically in later literature as a woman caught between conflicting loves and impossible duty. Her connections bind her to the heart of the tragedy: King Arthur, her husband, betrayed by her infidelity; Lancelot, the knight she loves, whose affair with her destroys Camelot; and Mordred, whose rebellion capitalized on the kingdom's internal fracture caused by her affair.
